tagline: Main Street houses trace Suffield from farming village to tobacco prosperity
intro: Route 75 follows North Street and Main Street through Suffield, where the northernmost 4.3 miles are a designated state scenic road. The village center stands on a ridge, with a green at the meeting of Main Street, Mountain Road and Bridge Street. Along Main Street, the historic district extends for 2.5 miles and contains buildings from the eighteenth through early twentieth centuries.

The road from Windsor through Poquonock to Suffield center was State Highway 362 in the 1920s. Renumbered Route 75 in 1932, it originally turned along Mapleton Avenue toward US 5A, now Route 159. The northward extension to Massachusetts came in 1950. Main Street already reflected an agricultural town whose prosperity grew after tobacco arrived in the early nineteenth century. Main Street lots had comparatively narrow frontage because frontage determined taxation, yet generally offered enough width for several homes. Large commercial and industrial developments remained uncommon along the village street.

Travel south from the Massachusetts line on North Street, continuing onto North Main and South Main through the center. King's Field House stands north of the village. Near the central junction, the Baptist church is Greek Revival and the Congregational church Romanesque Revival. Continue south past Hatheway House and Alexander King House on South Main Street.

moments.title: King's Field House
moments.text: The long rear roof of King's Field House descends to the first floor, giving it a saltbox profile. Lieutenant William King built the house about 1723, after receiving the surrounding acreage in 1722. Later generations of the family lived here and operated businesses including a blacksmith shop and a cooperage. The building contains several stages of eighteenth-century work, from its early timber framing to Georgian parlor paneling and a later entrance with a false fanlight. Delphina Hammer Clark restored the house in the 1930s. Its clapboard exterior and central chimney accompany the long roof, while a modern gabled addition projects behind the main block.
moments.notice: The rear roof slopes down to the first floor, forming the saltbox profile.

moments.title: Hatheway House
moments.text: Hatheway House grew in sections, with a central block, an older southern ell and a northern addition from 1795. Oliver Phelps bought the house from Shem Burbank in 1788 and transformed its decoration. Asher Benjamin designed the Doric portico added in 1795, which shelters the main entrance. Phelps was a principal in the six-million-acre Phelps and Gorham Purchase in upstate New York. In 1802 he moved to Canandaigua to oversee development and sale of his holdings more closely. Each section has a gambrel roof and wooden clapboards; a carriage house and barn also remain on the property.
moments.notice: The main entrance sits beneath Asher Benjamin’s Doric portico.

moments.title: Alexander King House
moments.text: At 232 South Main Street, Alexander King House retains Georgian paneling and cabinetry on both sides of its central chimney. Alexander King, a Yale graduate who practiced medicine in Suffield, built the house in 1764. He served as a town selectman and state legislator, then as a delegate to the Connecticut convention that ratified the United States Constitution in 1788. The Suffield Historical Society now operates the house as a museum. Outside, a central doorway framed by pilasters and a multilight transom sits in the five-bay clapboard facade, beneath a gabled roof.
